title: Students of Our Students’ Hearts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teachers should become deep students of how students' hearts work, rather than chasing each new fad. Opening with Augustine's line that life change comes from the loves of the heart, he ties it to the social-psychological finding that students who value school or a subject do the work, and do it with care. He contends that confusion about motivation fuels a churn of initiatives that shrinks the teaching profession into a short-term-missions mentality. His remedy is sustained study of beliefs about schooling and learning, which also frees teachers from fatalism about kids who just do not care. The post closes with a registration notice for his motivation course.
points: Lasting student change is inside-out: it depends on helping students come to believe five key things, not on exerting will.
Augustine's insight that the heart's loves drive change anticipates what researchers now show, that valuing a subject predicts careful work.
Chasing the next new thing shrinks the profession by encouraging a short-term-missions mentality instead of a lifelong commitment to teaching.
Studying how beliefs form and can be molded replaces fatalistic labels like 'that kid just doesn't care' with a more hopeful puzzle to solve.
Humble-boldness, a high view of teacher impact paired with an honest sense of limits, is one of the inside jobs of teaching.
quotes: Teaching toward the long-term flourishing of our students means that, in many cases, we desire that the lives of our students will change. We hold both a high view of the impact we can have — even obstacles like hard home lives aren't impenetrable — and a real sense of our lack of omnipotence. This internal balance is one of the key inside jobs of teaching; humble-boldness is inseparable from lasting greatness in education, be it in a classroom or as a leader.

Over this most recent school year, one of my chief takeaways from reading, teaching, and writing is that the life change we desire for our students is an inside-out thing. In short, we must help our students to believe five key things. I say it again and again, and I intend to keep doing so for as many years as I'm able.
I think that not understanding the mechanics at the root of our students' hearts is a key cause of our great confusion in education.

I think that what happens is that it shrinks and shrivels. Fewer and fewer people see teaching as a lifelong pursuit; more and more have a “short-term missions trip” mentality — I'm going to go and help the kids for a bit, and then I'll enter my career. Woe to us, I say, when the hardhats-and-work-boots work of promoting the long-term good of our nation's young becomes an extended service project.

So rather than constantly chasing after the next fad, I would argue that we need to become deep and earnest students of how our students' hearts — and our own hearts — work. We need to think about things like motivation at a level deeper than “intrinsic” or “extrinsic.” We need to study beliefs about schooling and learning: how these beliefs form, how they can be molded.
And I would dare say that this kind of study makes us wiser, deeper people — people who can much more quickly say, “My, what a fascinating puzzle,” when they're up against a motivational problem.
